hero.headline: Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties face potential losses of hundreds of millions under property tax reform
hero.teaser: Counties across the Treasure Coast are assessing the impact of a new property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills, with losses estimated in the hundreds of millions.
hero.body:
A recent study from the Florida Association of Counties estimates Martin County could lose $50 million in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29. St. Lucie County faces potential losses of $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29. Indian River County could lose $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29.

Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said if property taxes are cut, there will be real shortfalls and challenges, and revenue will have to be made up somewhere. Options like finding new revenue through increased sales tax or user fees for services and budget cuts are possibilities.

The referendum to raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 will be decided by voters in November. State Rep. Toby Overdorf from Stuart said the proposal is a break for the struggling family in a $300,000 home working several jobs to make ends meet.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce pastor accused of abusing five foster children in her home
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce pastor faces charges after police discovered alleged child abuse, starvation and filthy conditions inside her home.
cards.body:
Police arrested a Fort Pierce pastor on charges of abusing five foster children living in her home. Officers discovered alleged child abuse, starvation and filth during an investigation at the residence.

The pastor faces multiple charges related to the alleged abuse of the children in her care. Authorities removed the five foster children from the home following the discovery.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Pastor Charged with Child Neglect
cards.body:
A Fort Pierce pastor faces child neglect charges after children in her care were found in deplorable conditions, according to authorities.

The charges were filed Saturday after an investigation into the conditions where the youngsters were being kept.

The pastor was taken into custody following the discovery of the children in unsuitable living conditions.

Authorities have not released additional details about the number of children involved or the specific nature of the conditions discovered.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds receives death threats during Florida gubernatorial campaign, cites mental health concerns
cards.teaser: Gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds disclosed receiving death threats as he campaigns for the Republican nomination in the August primary.
cards.body:
Gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds is speaking out about threats on his life as he runs for the Republican nomination in the August primary. The Naples Republican, in his third term in Congress, faced one threat on social media last month after re-sharing President Donald Trump's endorsement in the Governor's race. A second person called Donalds' district office making similar threats, saying he was going to blow up the entire office. "Somebody just flat out said they were going to kill me," Donalds told radio host Mark Levin on Friday.

Donalds cited the assassination of conservative Charlie Kirk last year as an example of what happens when opponents are demonized rather than treated as human beings. He noted that while people have strong opinions in politics, demonizing opponents to the point of suggesting they will destroy Florida creates an opening for people with real mental health issues to commit violence. Though Donalds considers himself a free speech absolutist, he stressed the importance of being mindful of how things are said to avoid creating an environment where someone takes it upon themselves to harm another person. "That's just reprehensible to me," he said. The incident has strengthened his resolve to work hard to become governor and keep Florida the preeminent conservative state in America, and he remains undeterred by the threats.

cards.headline: Martin County fights 120-acre brush fire in Indiantown
cards.teaser: Martin County crews are battling a 120-acre brush fire in Indiantown.
cards.body:
The fire was reported Sunday in the Indiantown area. Crews are actively working to extinguish the blaze.

This fire comes after Martin County Fire Rescue extinguished a separate nearly 40-acre brush fire in Indiantown on Friday.

cards.headline: 18-year-old man charged with shooting 17-year-old girl in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: An 18-year-old man faces charges after allegedly shooting a 17-year-old girl in Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police arrested an 18-year-old man accused of shooting a 17-year-old girl. The shooting occurred Saturday in Fort Pierce.

The suspect is in custody facing charges related to the shooting.

cards.headline: 18-Year-Old Accused of Shooting Teenage Girl in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: An 18-year-old man faces charges after allegedly shooting a 17-year-old girl in Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
The shooting occurred Saturday afternoon, according to authorities.

The suspect was taken into custody and faces charges related to the incident.

hero.headline: 35 foster youth graduate at ChildNet celebration at Palm Beach State College
hero.teaser: ChildNet honored 35 students at its annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College, marking a milestone for foster youth and young adults served by the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit.
hero.body:
Thirty-five foster youth and young adults celebrated their graduation at an annual ceremony held by ChildNet at Palm Beach State College. The event marked an important milestone for students served by the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit organization. ChildNet provides comprehensive support to foster children and young adults through educational programs, adoption services, and resources for independent living.

Two graduates highlighted at the celebration were Sabrina Diaz and Brian Saintfort, both of whom experienced the loss of a parent and sought assistance from ChildNet during their challenging times. The organization provided them with the tools and resources needed to overcome their circumstances and continue their education. Diaz is pursuing pre-med coursework at Palm Beach State College with aspirations of becoming a physician. Saintfort has chosen a different path, enrolling in a vocational program to become a plumber. Both young adults credited their success to perseverance and belief in themselves.

Diaz shared advice for other young people facing similar hardships. She emphasized the importance of maintaining confidence in future success and dedicating effort toward achieving personal goals. Most critically, she stressed the need to stay committed to education and never abandon one's dreams, even when confronted with painful circumstances. "Belief that you're going to be big one day and just put effort into it, never give up on school and never give up on dreams. If you like push past with the pain and just keep trying hard," Diaz said. Saintfort delivered a similar message to his peers, reinforcing the power of self-belief and determination. "Believe that you'll make it, then you're gonna make it and stuff," Saintfort said.

Larry N. Rein, CEO of ChildNet, reflected on the meaning behind the graduation celebration and acknowledged the collective effort that made these student successes possible. He recognized the contributions of case workers employed by ChildNet and the Department of Children and Family Services, while placing special emphasis on the dedication of the graduates themselves. "This evening is the fruition of great work by everyone in the community, including case workers at ChildNet, DCF and especially the kids who have worked so hard. We are to celebrate them!" Rein said. The ceremony served as a testament to the organization's mission and the resilience of young people overcoming adversity through education and community support.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island erosion threatens to split island at Peck Lake, state report warns
cards.teaser: Nearly the entire coastline of Jupiter Island is critically eroded, with the ocean threatening to break through at Peck Lake and potentially split the island in half, according to a new state report.
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely that the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half. The threat stretches from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake. A storm previously breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. At risk is the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site already half lost to erosion, along with wildlife refuges including Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. According to Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society, there are over 33 threatened and endangered species in those areas.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town completed a major beach renourishment project in April 2025, dumping enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. About $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment every year. Field said oceanfront homes are not in immediate danger only because of ongoing erosion work. He cautioned that if funding for beach renourishment in Florida were to disappear, "the coastline of Florida is going to change very quickly, and not in a way that anybody's particularly happy with."

cards.headline: Florida could ban Fourth of July fireworks statewide due to extreme drought
cards.teaser: State leaders are considering banning fireworks for the Fourth of July's 250th anniversary celebration as Florida faces drought conditions more severe than 1998, the last time a statewide ban was enacted.
cards.body:
The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services says this year's drought is more severe than 1998, when the state last implemented a statewide fireworks ban. The entire state of Florida is at least abnormally dry, with areas including Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast experiencing moderate to extreme drought conditions. Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson issued an early warning in May about the possibility of a ban, stating that if drought conditions persist through Fourth of July, a ban would likely follow. Simpson acknowledged the significance of the 250th anniversary celebration but urged residents to consider alternatives.

At Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach, owner Bill Murphy said the store has already seen increased customer activity ahead of the holiday, with more people shopping early. Murphy said the store monitors drought conditions carefully but remains cautiously optimistic, noting there is plenty of rain in the forecast. The Department of Agriculture said a fireworks ban would be a last resort.

cards.headline: Florida voters divided on property tax ballot measure ahead of November vote
cards.teaser: Florida voters will decide in November whether to raise the homestead exemption and roll back property taxes, a proposal that needs 60% approval to pass and is drawing mixed reactions from residents.
cards.body:
Florida voters will decide this November whether to raise the homestead exemption for homeowners, a proposal that needs 60% approval to pass. A similar proposal to raise the homestead exemption failed in 2018.

Support for the measure is mixed among West Palm Beach residents. Brian Edington said he supports the idea because it benefits people who permanently live in Florida and saves homeowners money. He said he is comfortable with local governments spending less and pointed to his neighborhood's trash services, which pick up twice a week but could run once weekly, as an example of where cuts could be made. However, renters expressed skepticism about the measure. One resident along Clematis Avenue in downtown West Palm Beach said property owners will raise rent on renters, meaning the savings would not reach tenants. Rosabella Olivares expressed concern about reduced funding, noting that everything is expensive now.

cards.headline: Florida shark diving operators fight federal feeding ban in state waters
cards.teaser: A federal proposal to ban shark feeding within 200 miles of Florida's coast has cleared the U.S. House, drawing sharp criticism from dive operators who warn it could devastate conservation-driven tourism businesses.
cards.body:
Florida's shark diving industry is fighting a federal proposal to ban shark feeding off the state's coast. The measure, H.R. 3831, known as the Safe Florida Seas Act, would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said Congress has not asked operators to present data or explain their practices. Operators say they avoid surface chumming and instead take bait underwater during dives, which they argue is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats looking for food, unlike some commercial harvesting operations that release hundreds of gallons of chum at the surface.

In his letter to Congress, Campbell is urging senators to delay action, gather research and involve all stakeholders in shaping new rules. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a near perfect safety record for customers. Campbell said the industry is not scared of accountability and is requesting the chance to speak and share the science and facts with lawmakers. The bill cites Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters as precedent, but Florida operators argue that since Hawaii's ban, shark incidents have increased.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County rental assistance applications fill within hours as demand outweighs funding
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program receives about 600 applications in the first couple of hours each month, but demand far outweighs the nearly $2 million in available grant funding.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program is overwhelmed by demand that far exceeds available funding. The Community Services Department has nearly $2 million in combined grant funding but receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month combined with 211 data. Dr. James Green, program director, explained that the county currently has about 800 applications in the queue for rental assistance. Applications open at the beginning of each month and typically receive about 600 applications within the first couple of hours. At the time of this report, the county's assistance portal was marked closed due to high demand. Green said the recent surge in applications is partly due to rising costs of living, including housing, gas, and food.

According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 a month. Joanne Bromfield, who recently moved to West Palm Beach from Tampa, switched careers from a 12-year career as an educator to real estate hoping for a higher income. She said she worries about paying rent almost every day. For those in need, Green urges residents to call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check for availability. For those who cannot access the county's program, 211 is available 24/7 to connect residents with nonprofits and other assistance programs.

cards.headline: Fertilizer ban begins June 1 in Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties
cards.teaser: Residents in Martin, St.
cards.body:
Residents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties must stop using fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen on their lawns and landscaping. Jordan Skaggs, with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, said the ban helps reduce nutrient-rich runoff during the rainy season, which can cause algae blooms in local waterways like the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River.

According to Skaggs, these harmful algae blooms can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife. At certain densities, the blooms can release toxins that affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health. Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as a good alternative during the ban. Ricketts said residents can use a small trash can for composting, describing it as the easiest and most practical way to add nutrients to landscaping.

cards.headline: Fertilizer ban takes effect June 1 in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties to reduce harmful algae blooms
cards.teaser: A seasonal ban on fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen begins June 1 across three Treasure Coast counties to help reduce nutrient runoff during the rainy season.
cards.body:
Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties have implemented a ban on any fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen, effective June 1. Jordan Skaggs, with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, said the ban is designed to help reduce nutrient-rich runoff during the rainy season, which can cause algae blooms that disrupt waterways like the Indian River lagoon and St. Lucie River.

According to Skaggs, algae blooms can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife. At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health. Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as a good alternative during the ban for gardens and landscaping. Ricketts said a small trash can is the easiest and most practical way to add nutrients to your landscape.

cards.headline: Okeechobee County woman sues Campbell Soup and Walmart claiming worms found in SpaghettiOs
cards.teaser: Mary Hubbard from Okeechobee County filed a lawsuit seeking $50,000 in damages after she says she and her daughter found live worms in SpaghettiOs and developed parasitic infections.
cards.body:
Mary Hubbard of Okeechobee County claims she and her daughter found live worms in SpaghettiOs they purchased at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee in June 2024. According to the complaint, both she and her daughter developed parasitic infections and other medical complications after eating the product. Hubbard's attorneys said she discovered what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving within the food and documented the contamination in multiple videos that clearly depict worm-like organisms moving within the food product.

The lawsuit, which seeks $50,000 in damages, alleges that Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart failed to properly inspect the product. Campbell Soup Co. said the claims lack merit, while Walmart said it is reviewing the court filing.

cards.headline: Indian River Mall demolition underway as crews begin first phase of mixed-use redevelopment in Vero Beach
cards.teaser: Crews began demolishing portions of Indian River Mall this week to make way for a revitalization project that will transform the shopping center into a modern m.
cards.body:
Crews began demolishing portions of Indian River Mall this week as part of a revitalization project to transform the shopping center. Joseph Scarfone, the project manager for the redevelopment, said the first phase involves taking down the Macy's building and the former Sears location.

Neighbors gathered in the parking lot to watch the demolition. Mary Alice Stopyra said she was happy to see the mall torn down, noting it had degraded over time. Mark Manera, a Vero Beach resident who has visited the mall for years, described it as a graveyard that experienced a steady decline year after year. Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a new sleek and modern indoor and outdoor shopping center with around 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants and possible residential spaces. He described the project as "a city within a city" that will replace what has been a dead mall collecting cobwebs for the last 12 years. Scarfone said he hopes the first phase can be completed by 2027, with the development team continuing to work on permitting for the rest of the project.

cards.headline: Florida dive operators fight federal shark feeding ban, warn it could devastate conservation tourism
cards.teaser: A federal proposal to ban shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida is drawing criticism from dive operators who say it could devastate their businesses while doing little to improve safety.
cards.body:
The Safe Florida Seas Act, also known as H.R. 3831, cleared the U.S. House and would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. Supporters have called it a common-sense safety measure to reduce human-shark interactions. However, a coalition of dive operators argues the bill unfairly targets their work, which includes veteran-owned small businesses and nonprofits focused on education and conservation. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said no one from Congress has yet asked dive operators to present data or explain their practices. "What we're really requesting is the chance to speak and share the science and the facts," Campbell said.

Operators say they avoid surface chumming and instead take bait underwater during dives, which they argue is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats for food unlike some commercial harvesting operations that can release hundreds of gallons of chum at the surface. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a "near perfect safety record" for customers. Industry members note that since Hawaii banned shark feeding in 2006, shark incidents have increased and fatalities have been reported. Campbell is urging senators to delay action, gather research and involve all stakeholders in shaping any new rules.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County rental assistance program overwhelmed with 8,000 calls monthly as demand outweighs funding
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program receives about 600 applications within the first couple hours of opening each month, with nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance recorded monthly.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Community Services Department has nearly $2 million in combined grant funding for its Emergency Rental Assistance Program, designed to help residents who can't pay rent. However, demand significantly outweighs available resources. According to program director Dr. James Green, the county receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month based on combined data with 211, and currently has about 800 applications in the queue for rental assistance. Applications open at the beginning of each month but fill quickly, with the program typically receiving about 600 applications within the first couple of hours they're open. At the time of reporting, the county's assistance portal was marked closed due to high demand. Green urges anyone in need to call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check for availability.

Rising costs of living have intensified the crisis. According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 a month. Joanne Bromfield, who recently moved to West Palm Beach from Tampa, switched careers from education to real estate just to afford rent and said she worries about paying rent almost every day. Green cited rising housing, gas, and food costs as partly responsible for the recent surge in applications. For those unable to access the county program, 211 offers another option available 24/7 to connect residents with nonprofits and other assistance programs in the area.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island erosion threatens to split island at Peck Lake, putting wildlife refuges and archaeological sites at risk
cards.teaser: A new state report warns that nearly the entire coastline of Jupiter Island is critically eroded, with the ocean potentially breaking through at Peck Lake and splitting the island in half.
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that Jupiter Island's entire 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely that ocean water could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half by turning a thin strip of land into an open inlet. The threat stretches from Blowing Rocks Preserve, where private development is already at risk, to Peck Lake. A storm previously breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers refilled it with sand. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society warned that a future breach could upend ecosystems that depend on a delicate balance of fresh and saltwater to survive. Perry noted there are over 33 threatened and endangered species in the affected areas. A second state assessment warned that erosion threatens mangrove swamps critical for habitat and coastal protection, while rising water levels could displace entire species on the island.

Among the sites at risk is the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site already half lost to erosion, along with Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town fights erosion through constant maintenance. In April 2025, the town completed a beach renourishment project adding sand equivalent to nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. The town spends about $3 million annually in taxpayer dollars on beach renourishment. Field warned that if funding for beach renourishment disappeared, a breach could require massive state and federal investment for repairs.

hero.headline: 100 Paddlers to Cross 80 Miles of Ocean to Lake Worth Beach for Cystic Fibrosis
hero.teaser: More than 100 paddlers will launch from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13 and arrive at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling in the annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis.
hero.body:
The 80-mile endurance trek across the open Atlantic Ocean benefits the Pipers Angels Foundation, established by event founder Travis Suit in honor of his daughter Piper, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4. The fundraiser expects participants from around the world, and all paddlers must raise at least $2,000 for the cause. Crew or virtual participants have a $500 minimum, with final contributions due July 31.

The crossing is part of a four-day schedule beginning June 10 with arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove. On Thursday, participants take part in a 4Ocean beach cleanup and a community buffet dinner. Friday brings a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony to honor cystic fibrosis warriors, followed by rest and safety checks before launch night.

All paddlers are required to wear a U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation device, waterproof whistle, and reflective gear during dark hours. GPS trackers provided by the event must be worn and active at all times, and mandatory safety meetings will be held. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 to cheer paddlers during a daylong beach celebration marking their arrival. More information is available at crossingforcysticfibrosis.com and pipersangels.org.

cards.headline: Beetlejuice Musical Closes Today at West Palm Beach's Kravis Center
cards.body:
The Broadway musical "Beetlejuice" brings Tim Burton's 1988 film to life at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach through June 7. Actor Ryan Stajmiger plays the mischievous demon in the iconic striped suit, delivering the spooky humor and over-the-top visuals at the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a "strange and unusual" teen whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble. Stajmiger has been a longtime fan of the source material. "I've loved the movie since I was a kid. I'm a huge Tim Burton fan, and you know, Michael Keaton's performance is so iconic," he told WPTV. He noted that Keaton's role in the original film lasted only 15 minutes but left a lasting impression.

One aspect Stajmiger especially enjoys is the direct connection with the audience through breaking the fourth wall. "I get to break the fourth wall a lot, so I get to communicate directly to the audience and share some moments with them. That's my favorite part of theater," he explained. Early in the run, an unexpected moment added spontaneity to a performance when his second wig came off along with the first during a wig change, leaving him bald for an entire scene. Rather than breaking character, Stajmiger played with the moment and experienced the audience's reaction. Performances continue through June 7, with shows at 7:30 p.m. on June 3 and 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, and matinee and evening performances on June 6. Tickets start at $34.50 at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up with parental discretion advised.

hero.headline: Byron Donalds calls for GOP unity ahead of Florida gubernatorial primary as opponents demand debates
hero.teaser: Naples Republican Byron Donalds says the party should unite behind him more than two months before the August 18 primary, following the departure of Democrat Jerry Demings from his party's race.
hero.body:
Byron Donalds declared Friday that the general election has effectively begun following Jerry Demings' withdrawal from the Democratic primary for Governor due to a prostate cancer diagnosis. The Naples Republican, who has raised $81 million, argued that Republicans should unite behind his candidacy more than two months before the August 18 primary election. With Democrats having a presumptive nominee in the wake of Demings' departure, Donalds said he would rather direct his substantial financial resources toward the general election than continue competing in the Republican primary.

Donalds pointed to his complete and total endorsement from President Donald Trump and his lead of more than 40 points in multiple public polls as evidence of his viability as the party's nominee. He contrasted his record with that of his Democratic opponent, saying the differences between himself and David Jolly could not be more stark. Jolly would end the Florida Dream and transform the state into another Virginia, Illinois, California, or New York, Donalds said, referencing the migration of residents fleeing blue state governance. He called on the Republican party to unite and focus on defending Governor DeSantis's accomplishments and keeping Florida free.

Rather than participate in debates, Donalds said he would continue engaging voters through direct contact methods including town halls, community meetings, business roundtables, and door-to-door canvassing. He noted that all other candidates remain in single digits and argued that fighting amongst Republicans only helps Democrats achieve their goals. My campaign is committed to town halls, community meetings, business roundtables, and door knocking to take our message of conservatism and common sense directly to the people of Florida, Donalds said.

Donalds' debate avoidance has drawn criticism from opponents. Jay Collins launched The Collins Callout website Friday, writing that the only question left is whether Byron answers the bell, or keeps running. Former House Speaker Paul Renner posted a video to social media urging Donalds to stop ducking and get on stage, stating that Floridians deserve to see the differences between candidates. Renner also said neither Collins nor Donalds has been willing to debate him. Updated fundraising reports covering activity through May are due June 10. Through the end of March, Renner had raised more than $6 million while Collins had raised roughly $1.75 million.

cards.headline: Tampa City Council Chair seeks delay on Rays stadium CRA vote as negotiations continue
cards.teaser: Tampa City Council Chair Alan Clendenin is pushing to delay a Community Redevelopment Agency discussion tied to the Tampa Bay Rays stadium proposal until July or later.
cards.body:
Tampa City Council Chair Alan Clendenin submitted a memo last week requesting that the Rays stadium item be deferred from next week's Tampa CRA meeting until at least July, and possibly longer. He said behind-the-scenes negotiations are still ongoing and recent uncertainty over property tax reform has added another factor for negotiators to consider. Clendenin sharply disputed Hillsborough County Commissioner Joshua Wostal's characterization of where negotiations stand, saying "Josh Wostal has no idea what's happening. Zero."

The Rays stadium MOU approved by Tampa and Hillsborough County last month includes $80 million from the city of Tampa and another $100 million tied to the Tampa CRA, in addition to other public dollars. Clendenin said the earlier votes by the City Council and County Commission represented support for the general direction of the non-binding MOU, but not final approval of the CRA terms. Several options remain on the table for the CRA-related portion of the deal, including not using the CRA, creating a different type of district or using another special district structure. For the CRA portion, nothing has been agreed to by any party, Clendenin said. He acknowledged that many details remain behind closed doors but said that is unavoidable while negotiations are ongoing.

cards.headline: Former Lake County Property Appraiser Carey Baker launches congressional campaign in CD 11
cards.teaser: Carey Baker is running to succeed retiring U.S. Representative Daniel Webster in a GOP Primary that includes Lake County Commissioner Anthony Sabatini.
cards.body:
Former Lake County Property Appraiser Carey Baker is running for U.S. Congress in Florida's 11th Congressional District. The 63-year-old represented much of Central Florida in both the Florida House and Senate before being elected countywide as Property Appraiser. Baker lost his re-election bid in 2024 after filing as a write-in candidate, defeated by Republican David Jordan by a 3-to-1 margin in the General Election. Despite the loss, Baker raised $233,000 for his campaign, demonstrating fundraising strength for the GOP primary race. He will face Lake County Commissioner Anthony Sabatini, a onetime protégé who has previously run for the seat. Following the 2024 election loss, Baker worked with Sabatini in an unsuccessful effort to become Lake County Republican Party Chair. A lifelong Eustis resident, Baker has remained a high-profile Republican leader in Lake County since his 2000 election to the Florida House. His father also served the area in the Florida House.

Florida's 11th Congressional District includes all of Sumter County, most of Lake County, and some of west Orange County. The district leans heavily Republican, with more than 57% of voters supporting President Donald Trump in the 2024 Presidential Election. On the Democratic side, repeat candidate Barbie Harden Hall suspended her campaign Saturday due to health issues. Hall was the leading fundraiser among Democratic candidates but will no longer seek the nomination. Three other candidates, Royal Webster, Shawn Bettis, and Dan Williams, remain in the Democratic race.

cards.headline: Jacksonville Democrat Benjamin Sandlin launches second run for HD 12 after 2024 loss
cards.teaser: Benjamin Sandlin filed Friday for the Jacksonville House race, just three days before qualifying begins Monday, June 8.
cards.body:
Democrat Benjamin Sandlin is launching a second run for Jacksonville's House District 12 seat after losing by 14 points to House Speaker Pro Tempore Wyman Duggan two years ago. The Republican-leaning district is open because Duggan is term-limited. The 22-year-old filed for the House race Friday, three days before qualifying began Monday, June 8. Sandlin said the Florida Democratic Party and he agreed the seat was too close in 2024 to leave uncontested, calling it a missed opportunity for an extra voice on labor rights, public schools and housing justice in the Legislature. As the sole Democrat in HD 12, Sandlin is likely to advance to the November ballot upon qualifying.

Sandlin previously filed for the race to succeed Democrat Jimmy Peluso in City Council District 7, as Peluso launched a run for an at-large seat. After Sandlin dropped out, the District 7 race remained crowded with six Democrats and a no party affiliation candidate on the ballot. Former Jacksonville City Council President Terrance Freeman is also running in HD 12 to succeed Duggan. Through the end of May, Freeman raised more than $167,000 to his campaign account and an additional $506,000 to an affiliated political committee called For the Future We Want, leaving him with roughly $390,000 on hand. Freeman was appointed to Jacksonville City Council in 2018 by former Governor Rick Scott to fill a vacancy, then elected to at-large seats in 2019 and 2023.

cards.headline: Rick Scott honors father's D-Day service as World War II veteran
cards.teaser: Senator Rick Scott remembered his adopted father Orba Scott, who parachuted behind enemy lines during the 1944 D-Day operation in Normandy.
cards.body:
Senator Rick Scott is keeping the memory of World War II alive. On Saturday, the Naples Republican and Navy veteran remembered what many members of the military had to do on D-Day, the famous 1944 World War II military operation wherein more than 160,000 Allied troops stormed the beaches of Normandy and made first headway in the liberation of German-occupied France. Orba Scott, who raised the Senator, was among those engaged in the operation. As the Senator recounts, his adopted dad parachuted behind enemy lines and selflessly fought for the well-being and freedom of Americans and families across the world.

"My father was blessed enough to return home from battle, but many brave individuals made the last full measure of devotion in defense of freedom and didn't return home," Scott said. As a Senator, a Navy veteran and the son of an Army veteran, Scott vows to continue fighting for those who have fought for America. "I am fighting every day to improve our military, take care of our nation's veterans, and protect your legacy so the next generation knows and appreciate the sacrifices made for their freedoms," he said.

cards.headline: Former Cuban President Raúl Castro appears publicly after U.S. indictment for 1996 aircraft downing
cards.teaser: Raúl Castro appeared in public for the first time since being indicted by the United States for his alleged role in the 1996 downing of two civilian aircraft.
cards.body:
Raúl Castro made a rare public appearance Friday night at a celebration of his 95th birthday held at the Ministry of Interior in Havana, marking his first public outing since being indicted by the United States. State TV broadcast footage showing Castro, dressed in his olive-green military uniform, entering a packed theater to a standing ovation alongside his grandson and bodyguard Raúl Guillermo Rodríguez and Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel. The event offered Cuba's socialist government an opportunity to close ranks and project defiance as the Trump administration escalates pressure on the fuel-starved island.

Díaz-Canel delivered an effusive tribute to Castro and his late brother Fidel Castro, praising Raúl Castro's "heroism and dignity" and his nearly 50 years as Cuba's defense minister. Díaz-Canel highlighted Castro's "courage and loyalty" that made him a target for enemy intelligence services, declaring "Raúl is Cuba, and Cuba is untouchable," echoing slogans that have appeared on Havana billboards and social media since the May 20 U.S. indictment. The Justice Department indictment accuses Castro of ordering the 1996 shootdown of civilian planes flown by Miami-based exiles. Although Castro formally retired from politics in April 2021, he is believed to wield considerable political power.

hero.headline: Stuart unveils mural promoting ecosystem awareness
hero.teaser: Stuart has unveiled a large mural designed to promote awareness of local ecosystems.
hero.body:
The mural was unveiled as part of efforts to educate residents about environmental conservation. The artwork is now on display in Stuart.

Details about the specific location and the artists involved were not provided.

The improvements to the dispatch center were completed Saturday. The facility handles emergency calls for Martin County.

The revamped center is now operational serving the county's emergency response needs.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue puts out 40-acre Indiantown brush fire

cards.body:
The fire was contained and put out Friday evening. Fire crews worked to prevent the blaze from spreading further.

The Indiantown fire was brought under control without reported injuries or structural damage.

The chase slowed traffic flow on the highway. The pursuit was brief and concluded near the Hobe Sound area.

Northbound I-95 traffic was affected during the incident.

cards.headline: 35 foster youth graduate at ChildNet celebration
cards.teaser: Thirty-five foster youth walked across the stage at ChildNet's annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College.
cards.body:
ChildNet held its annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College, where 35 foster youth and young adults walked across the stage to mark a significant milestone. The Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit supports foster kids and young men and women through education, adoptions and independent living resources.

Among the graduates were Sabrina Diaz and Brian Saintfort, both of whom lost a parent and turned to ChildNet for support. The organization equipped them with the resources they needed to move forward. Diaz is already enrolled in pre-med classes at Palm Beach State College, where she hopes to become a doctor. Saintfort plans to pursue a vocational program to become a plumber. Larry N. Rein, CEO of ChildNet, reflected on the evening's significance, saying "This evening is the fruition of great work by everyone in the community, including case workers at ChildNet, DCF and especially the kids who have worked so hard."

hero.headline: Fort Pierce pastor accused of abusing five foster children in her home
hero.teaser: A Fort Pierce pastor faces charges after police discovered alleged child abuse, starvation and filthy conditions inside her home.
hero.body:
Police arrested a Fort Pierce pastor on charges of abusing five foster children living in her home. Officers discovered alleged child abuse, starvation and filth during an investigation at the residence.

The pastor faces multiple charges related to the alleged abuse of the children in her care. Authorities removed the five foster children from the home following the discovery.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County fertilizer ban takes effect June 30 to protect waterways
cards.teaser: St.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County will ban the use of any fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen starting June 30. The ban also applies to Indian River and Martin counties and will remain in effect during the rainy season to reduce nutrient-rich runoff that can cause algae blooms in local waterways.

Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County said the ban helps protect the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River from harmful algae blooms. The blooms can shade out beneficial plants that fish and wildlife depend on. At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health. Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, said composting offers a good alternative during the ban for gardens and landscaping. A small trash can provides the easiest and most practical way to add nutrients to landscaping during the restricted period.

cards.headline: 18-year-old man charged with shooting 17-year-old girl in Fort Pierce

Fort Pierce police arrested an 18-year-old man accused of shooting a 17-year-old girl. The shooting occurred Saturday in Fort Pierce.

The suspect is in custody facing charges related to the shooting.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie to celebrate Juneteenth at MIDFLORIDA Event Center
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie will host a Juneteenth celebration at the MIDFLORIDA Event Center later this month.
cards.body:
The city of Port St. Lucie will hold a Juneteenth celebration at the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. The event marks the annual observance of Juneteenth on June 19, commemorating the end of slavery in the United States.

The MIDFLORIDA Event Center will serve as the venue for the Port St. Lucie community celebration. Details about the event schedule and activities were announced Saturday.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested after homeowner watches burglary on security camera
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie homeowner used security camera footage to help police arrest a masked intruder who stole a $300 watch from an apartment.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested a man after a homeowner spotted a burglary in progress on a security camera. The masked intruder broke into a Port St. Lucie apartment and stole a $300 watch.

The homeowner monitored the break-in through security camera footage and contacted police. Officers arrested the suspect following the burglary. Video evidence captured the masked intruder during the crime.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County woman charged with stealing $60,000 from bingo hall
cards.teaser: A St. Lucie County woman faces theft charges after allegedly stealing $60,000 from a bingo hall.
cards.body:
Police arrested a St. Lucie County woman accused of stealing $60,000 from a bingo hall. The woman faces grand theft charges in connection with the alleged theft.

Authorities investigated the missing funds at the bingo hall and identified the woman as a suspect. The suspect is in custody facing charges related to the $60,000 theft.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce port explores new space industry facility and other developments
cards.teaser: The Port of Fort Pierce is considering a new facility for the space industry as part of ongoing development plans.
cards.body:
The Port of Fort Pierce is exploring the addition of a new space industry facility. Port officials discussed the potential facility along with other port updates and development projects.

The space industry facility would mark a new direction for the Fort Pierce port. Officials continue to evaluate the proposal as part of broader port expansion and modernization efforts.

hero.headline: Flutie Brothers to perform free concert at Capt. Hirams Sandbar in Sebastian
hero.teaser: The Flutie Brothers will play their annual free concert at Capt. Hirams Sandbar in Sebastian.
hero.body:
Capt. Hirams Sandbar in Sebastian will host the Flutie Brothers for their annual free concert. The event continues a tradition at the waterfront venue.

The performance is open to the public at no charge. Capt. Hirams Sandbar is located in Sebastian on the Indian River.

cards.headline: Texas Rangers Youth Academy team debuts in Vero Beach June 17
cards.teaser: The Texas Rangers Youth Academy 2026 Breakthrough Series Invitational team will make its debut in Vero Beach on June 17.
cards.body:
The Texas Rangers Youth Academy is bringing its 2026 Breakthrough Series Invitational team to Vero Beach. The team is set to debut on June 17.

The event marks the arrival of the youth baseball program to the Treasure Coast. Vero Beach will host the invitational team as part of the Rangers' youth development initiative.

cards.headline: Vero Beach police chief defends search efforts for slaying suspect Jesse Ellis
cards.teaser: The Vero Beach police chief said officers did all they could to find slaying suspect Jesse Ellis.
cards.body:
The Vero Beach police chief said officers did all they could to find slaying suspect Jesse Ellis. The statement came Friday as questions arose about the search for Ellis.

Ellis is wanted in connection with a slaying in Vero Beach. The police chief addressed concerns about the department's efforts to locate the suspect.

The chief's comments came amid ongoing efforts to apprehend Ellis. The case remains active as authorities continue their search.

Vero Beach police have not announced any arrests in the case. The investigation continues as law enforcement works to locate Ellis.

cards.headline: Fertilizer ban now in effect across Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties
cards.teaser: A fertilizer ban is in place in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties.
cards.body:
Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties are under a fertilizer ban. The restriction applies across all three Treasure Coast counties.

The ban is part of water quality protection efforts in the region. Residents in Indian River County and neighboring counties must follow the fertilizer restrictions.

cards.headline: Dolphin fishing line entanglements surge in Indian River Lagoon
cards.teaser: Wildlife scientists report a skyrocketing number of dolphins entangled in fishing line in the Indian River Lagoon.
cards.body:
Wildlife scientists are expressing concern over a sharp increase in dolphin and fishing line cases in the Indian River Lagoon. The number of entanglement incidents has risen significantly.

The Indian River Lagoon runs along the Treasure Coast, including Indian River County. Scientists are monitoring the situation as fishing line continues to pose a threat to marine mammals in the lagoon.

cards.teaser: The Recycling Club of Indian River County announced 2026 college scholarship opportunities for students.

The Recycling Club of Indian River County is offering college scholarships for 2026. The organization announced the scholarship opportunities Friday.

Students in Indian River County can apply for the scholarships. The Recycling Club provides educational funding as part of its community programs.
